passages.t: ‘Sing to the LORD a new song’, and the double-edged sword
passages.happening:
Psalm 149 begins, “Hallelujah! Sing to the LORD a new song” (verse 1). The singing is for God's people together, “in the assembly of the godly” (verse 1). “Let Israel rejoice in their Maker; let the children of Zion rejoice in their King” (verse 2). “Let them praise His name with dancing, and make music to Him with tambourine and harp” (verse 3).

The reason: “For the LORD takes pleasure in His people; He adorns the afflicted with salvation” (verse 4). Let them sing for joy, even on their beds (verse 5).

Then the psalm changes tone. “May the high praises of God be in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands” (verse 6), to bring God's judgment on the nations and to bind their kings in chains (verses 7 and 8), “to execute the judgment written against them. This honor is for all His saints. Hallelujah!” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Worship in Israel was loud and physical. After the crossing of the sea, “Miriam the prophetess, Aaron's sister, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women followed her with tambourines and dancing” (Exodus 15:20).

‘He adorns the afflicted with salvation’ (verse 4) is a lovely picture: God dresses up the humble in rescue, as if putting fine clothes on them.

‘Upon their beds’ (verse 5) is unclear. It may mean praise that goes on at night, in private. It may mean the couches where people lay at a feast. Readers take it both ways.

Verses 6 to 9 are battle poetry from ancient Israel, a small people among great empires, who hoped God would judge the nations that crushed them. Many scholars date the psalm after the exile, when that hope was strong. Notice that verse 9 limits the action to ‘the judgment written’, God's own decree, not the people's own plans.
passages.later:
The New Testament speaks of a different sword. Paul tells believers to take up “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). Hebrews says, “For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword” (Hebrews 4:12).

When Peter drew a sword to defend Jesus, Jesus said, “Put your sword back in its place” (Matthew 26:52). Paul wrote, “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world” (2 Corinthians 10:4).
passages.hard: Do verses 6 to 9 give God's people a right to take up arms against other nations in his name? No. These lines are the battle poetry of ancient Israel, and they give no one today a warrant for violence of any kind. Such verses have at times been misused to defend religious violence, and that misuse was wrong. Christians read the church's ‘sword’ as the word of God (Ephesians 6:17; Hebrews 4:12), and leave judgment to Christ at his return. That is a reading, and it is how the New Testament itself turns the picture.
passages.asks:
Psalm 149 asks you to sing a new song: praise that is fresh, not just routine. What has God done lately that you have not thanked him for?

And it asks what is in your hands. For a Christian, the sword is God's word. Is it in your mouth and in your hands, to speak truth with love?
